strengths: The benchmark addresses a meaningful weakness in video MLLM evaluation: random distractors can substantially overestimate fine-grained action recognition. GPT-4o drops from 87.6% with random choices to 52.2% with TIM-generated distractors.

The in-domain improvements are substantial and demonstrated across three model backbones. At matched eight-frame input, LLaVAction improves LLaVA-Video-7B from 35.7% to 71.7%, exceeding GPT-4o's 52.2%. Training with AVION distractors and evaluating with TIM distractors provides useful evidence of transfer across distractor generators.

The paper includes cumulative and leave-one-out ablations, explicit training prompts, and evaluation on several external benchmarks. Using predicted rather than ground-truth previous actions during inference is an appropriate design choice.
weaknesses: The benchmark's validity is insufficiently established. Different action classes do not guarantee mutually exclusive natural-language descriptions, particularly when narrations are sampled from other clips and videos contain overlapping actions. There is no systematic human audit, human accuracy estimate, or text-only baseline to establish answer uniqueness and rule out linguistic shortcuts. Changing distractor generators within EPIC-KITCHENS supports a narrower generalization claim than the repeated 'OOD' framing suggests.

The standard action-recognition comparison needs a clearer evaluation protocol. Table 4 evaluates a TIM-plus-MLLM reranking pipeline, and its ground-truth-narration variants use instance-specific annotation information unavailable in ordinary classification. For the official-key results, the paper should explicitly confirm that evaluation never inserts the true class into TIM's top-20 candidates, report candidate recall and handling of missing targets, and compare against simpler reranking baselines. The reported 58.3% versus TIM's 56.4% is promising but does not establish the benefit of the proposed machinery cleanly.

External-benchmark improvements are confounded by additional training on LLaVA-Video-178K. There is no replay-only control with matched training budget or comparison against ordinary EPIC fine-tuning with the same replay. Consequently, Table 5 cannot isolate the contribution of the proposed techniques. Improvements are generally modest, NextQA decreases, and VideoMME action recognition and action reasoning both decline in the appendix.

The external evaluation contains a concrete reporting inconsistency. The 20 MVBench baseline accuracies in Table 9 average to 60.15%, while the proposed model averages to approximately 61.13%. Table 5 instead reports 58.6% versus 61.1%, inflating the apparent gain from approximately 1.0 to 2.5 points unless different evaluation configurations were used; none are explained.

Methodological novelty is limited and not adequately distinguished from established hard-negative mining, auxiliary classification, multitask instruction tuning, and temporal context conditioning. Several supposedly important additions have weak marginal support: removing vision supervision or GPT-4o distillation reduces the full model by only 0.3 or 0.2 points, respectively. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates establish these small effects, and adding prior-action learning actually reduces cumulative accuracy before test-time augmentation.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified, including auxiliary-loss weights, precise task and replay sampling proportions, and the exact narration sampling and candidate deduplication procedure. Extensive development on the same EPIC validation set, without a separate held-out confirmation, further limits confidence in the selected configuration and state-of-the-art claim.

strengths: The benchmark targets a meaningful weakness: distinguishing visually similar actions. Model-generated distractors substantially reduce accuracy compared with random choices; GPT-4o drops from 87.6% to 52.2% (Table 1).

The training recipe delivers substantial improvements on EPIC-KITCHENS-100-MQA across three backbones. At the same eight-frame input budget, LLaVAction-7B achieves 71.7%, versus 35.7% for its initial backbone and 52.2% for GPT-4o.

The paper includes random-distractor training baselines, incremental and leave-one-out ablations, cross-generator evaluation, and experiments on six additional benchmarks. Training prompts and several implementation details are provided.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity is insufficiently established. Excluding the ground-truth action class does not guarantee that sampled narrations are semantically incorrect or mutually exclusive, particularly for overlapping actions and synonymous object descriptions. No human ambiguity audit, agreement measurement, or text-only baseline establishes that the harder questions reliably measure visual action recognition.

The standard action-recognition comparison needs a more explicit protocol. Table 4 evaluates a TIM-plus-MLLM reranking system, rather than a standalone recognizer. It should explicitly establish that ground truth is never inserted at evaluation, explain how missing ground-truth candidates are handled, and report candidate recall and total inference cost. The ground-truth-narration variant also needs clarification regarding what instance-specific annotation is available at inference. These details matter because the MQA construction elsewhere explicitly guarantees inclusion of the correct answer.

The broader generalization gains are not cleanly attributable to the proposed methods. Table 5 uses additional training with LLaVA-Video-178K replay but lacks a matched replay-only continuation baseline and a simpler EPIC fine-tuning control. Improvements are mostly modest, NextQA declines, and VideoMME action recognition and action reasoning both decline in Table 11.

Numerical inconsistencies weaken confidence in the evaluation. The 20 MVBench baseline accuracies in Table 9 average 60.15%, rather than the 58.6% reported in Table 5; the proposed model averages approximately 61.1%, making the corresponding gain approximately 1.0 rather than 2.5 points. Removing prior-action learning yields 73.6% in Table 3 but 72.3% in Table 7 under apparently matching configurations. These discrepancies require reconciliation.

Methodological novelty is limited and insufficiently distinguished from established techniques. The approach combines hard-negative mining, supervised classification of an added token, temporal localization, caption distillation, and contextual prompting. The claimed vision-token supervision actually supervises an added action token at the final layer, and its effect on visual representations is not analyzed. Its leave-one-out contribution is only 0.3 points, substantially smaller than the highlighted incremental gain.

The evidence lacks an independent final evaluation and uncertainty estimates. The EPIC validation split supports benchmark construction, extensive method comparisons, and candidate-count selection, with no separate held-out result. Changing the distractor generator within the same dataset provides useful robustness evidence but only a narrow distribution shift. Repeated runs or confidence intervals are especially important for the small auxiliary-task gains; loss weights and replay proportions are also insufficiently specified.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a meaningful weakness in video MLLM evaluation: randomly sampled alternatives can make action recognition artificially easy. GPT-4o’s drop from 87.6% with random distractors to 52.2% with TIM distractors provides compelling evidence.
The training pipeline produces substantial improvements across three model backbones. At matched eight-frame inputs, LLaVAction reaches 71.7%, versus 35.7% for its base model and 52.2% for GPT-4o.

The paper includes incremental and leave-one-out ablations, comparisons between distractor generators, detailed prompts, and evaluations on six additional benchmarks. Training with AVION distractors and evaluating with TIM distractors is a useful robustness check.
weaknesses: The benchmark’s validity needs stronger verification. The correct option is the clip’s own narration, whereas distractors are narrations from other clips selected through action classes. Different classes do not guarantee semantically exclusive answers, especially for overlapping actions. Human agreement, ambiguity audits, and text-only controls are missing, leaving uncertainty about what the benchmark measures.

The standard action-recognition comparison is insufficiently specified. Table 4 uses TIM’s top-20 candidates, but does not explicitly establish whether ground-truth insertion used elsewhere is disabled during evaluation or explain handling of candidate-recall failures. The ground-truth-narration results additionally supply clip-specific annotation information unavailable in ordinary classification. These results cannot straightforwardly substantiate the headline state-of-the-art claim without a fully specified, label-independent inference protocol.

The methodological novelty is modest: hard-negative training, auxiliary classification, temporal localization, distillation, and action-history conditioning are established ideas. The paper demonstrates a useful combination but does not adequately distinguish its contributions from conventional multitask fine-tuning and candidate reranking.

Component attribution is less convincing than the main text suggests. Removing vision supervision reduces accuracy by only 0.3 points in Table 7, versus the highlighted 3.9-point incremental gain; removing distillation costs only 0.2 points. Table 3’s 73.6% before adding prior-action training also appears inconsistent with Table 7’s 72.3% without that component unless other settings differ. Multiple seeds and clarification are needed.

The transfer experiments introduce replay of LLaVA-Video-178K without a matched continued-training/replay baseline, so improvements cannot be attributed cleanly to the proposed techniques. Gains are often small, NextQA decreases, and VideoMME’s action-recognition and action-reasoning subsets both decline.

The strongest comparisons are against zero-shot models despite substantial supervised domain adaptation. Although the fine-tuning ablations are helpful, stronger matched-training baselines and an independent held-out evaluation would better establish significance. Changing distractor generators within EPIC-KITCHENS supports a narrower robustness claim than broad out-of-distribution generalization.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of video MLLMs: distinguishing closely related actions rather than recognizing broadly different activities. Specialist-generated distractors provide a practical, scalable benchmark construction strategy, and Table 1 convincingly demonstrates that random choices substantially overestimate performance.

Hard-distractor training produces substantial improvements beyond ordinary in-domain fine-tuning. Table 3 reports 64.4% accuracy with AVION distractors versus 55.0% with random distractors, while the complete model reaches 74.1%. Additive and leave-one-out ablations provide useful evidence about the individual components.

The experimental coverage is unusually broad, spanning several model backbones, four action-recognition datasets, and 13 general video benchmarks. Animal Kingdom results against random-choice fine-tuning provide particularly useful evidence that the approach extends beyond kitchen activities.

The structured prediction pipeline is practical and explicitly acknowledges its candidate-recall ceiling. The action-label result of 58.3% versus TIM's 56.4% suggests that the second-stage model adds useful discrimination beyond the specialist.
weaknesses: The strongest EPIC-KITCHENS action-recognition result has a serious evaluation concern. Section 4.3 states that the narration setting uses the narration of the corresponding video clip. This appears to introduce sample-specific ground-truth annotation into the inference choices, information unavailable in ordinary action recognition. The 63.2% result therefore does not establish a fair improvement over specialist classifiers without clarification and an annotation-independent candidate construction. The separate 58.3% action-label result is more credible.

Benchmark validity needs stronger controls. The correct choice uses the target clip's narration, whereas distractors use narrations from other clips and classes. This asymmetry could introduce linguistic or specificity cues, and different class labels do not guarantee mutually exclusive descriptions of a video. There is no reported human ambiguity audit, human performance estimate, or text-only baseline to establish how much accuracy measures visual action discrimination.

The OOD interpretation is overstated. Switching from AVION-generated training distractors to TIM-generated test distractors demonstrates transfer between candidate generators within the same dataset, rather than broad domain generalization. Appendix D's experiment changes both training and testing K, so decreasing accuracy cannot isolate overfitting from increased test difficulty. Its reported confidence interval for mean JSD also appears inconsistent with the stated mean, standard deviation, and sample count.

The architectural novelty and its causal support are limited. The action token closely resembles a classification token with auxiliary supervision, and removing it from the complete model decreases accuracy by only 0.5 points. Attention magnitudes do not establish improved causal use of visual evidence. Comparisons against pooled-feature auxiliary supervision and direct prediction with the already-trained classification heads would better establish the token's necessity and the need for an external specialist.

Generalization claims require qualification. EPFL zero-shot results apply only to the second-stage model and depend on a target-dataset-trained candidate generator; Meccano and Animal Kingdom involve target-domain fine-tuning. General video benchmark gains are often small, three benchmarks regress, and VideoMME action recognition and action reasoning both decline. Without uncertainty estimates or a replay-only control, these results more strongly support retaining general capabilities than consistently improving action understanding.

Several details needed for reproduction and fair attribution remain unclear, including task sampling proportions, replay mixing ratio, auxiliary-loss weights, and the exact multilabel candidate/output procedure for Animal Kingdom. End-to-end inference costs should include the specialist, and the headline 21-point comparison against GPT-4o uses different frame budgets. Overall, the practical gains are promising, but unresolved evaluation issues place the submission slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: fine-grained action discrimination is poorly measured by multiple-choice questions with random distractors. Specialist-generated distractors provide a practical construction method, and Table 1 clearly demonstrates their increased difficulty across several MLLMs.

The improvements extend beyond comparisons with zero-shot models. Training with hard distractors improves accuracy from 55.0% to 64.4% relative to random-distractor training in Table 3. Animal Kingdom experiments also show substantial improvements over models trained with random choices, including on a second model family.

Evaluation is broad, covering four action-recognition datasets and 13 video-language benchmarks. The standard action-label setting improves EPIC-KITCHENS accuracy from TIM’s 56.4% to 58.3%, and the EPFL and MECCANO results provide additional evidence of practical value.

The paper includes additive and leave-one-out ablations, alternative action-token designs, structured-output comparisons, training settings, and task prompts. These make the empirical investigation substantially more informative than a simple fine-tuning comparison.
weaknesses: The narration-based recognition result has a serious comparability concern. Section 4.3 explicitly uses the narration of the corresponding evaluation clip when constructing choices. This supplies annotation-derived, clip-specific information unavailable in ordinary action classification. The reported 63.2% should not be presented as directly comparable to specialist recognition accuracy without a candidate-generation protocol independent of evaluation annotations. The 58.3% action-label result is the more defensible comparison.

Benchmark validity needs stronger verification. The correct option uses the target clip’s narration, whereas distractors use narrations sampled from other clips and classes. Differences in specificity or wording could introduce shortcuts, while overlapping actions could create multiple plausible answers. There is no reported human agreement study, ambiguity audit, or text-only baseline establishing that performance primarily measures visual action discrimination.

The methodological novelty is relatively incremental: specialist-based hard-negative mining, multitask instruction tuning, an auxiliary classification token, and candidate reranking are familiar mechanisms. The action token contributes only 0.5 percentage points in the full-model leave-one-out ablation, despite its larger intermediate additive gain. Comparisons with pooled-feature auxiliary supervision and directly using the already-trained classification heads would better establish the architectural contribution.

The OOD interpretation is overstated. Changing the distractor generator from AVION to TIM establishes a change in candidate distribution, but does not establish broad domain generalization or eliminate shortcut learning. Appendix D changes the number of choices during both training and testing, so declining accuracy cannot isolate overfitting from increased test difficulty. Its reported JSD confidence interval also needs clarification, and the statistical test’s null hypothesis is unspecified.

The structured-recognition system depends on a trained specialist at inference. Although this dependency is disclosed, candidate recall ceilings, complete inference costs, and stronger matched reranking or ensemble baselines are missing. EPFL’s zero-shot result applies only to the second-stage model because candidate generation uses a target-domain specialist; it is not zero-shot transfer of the complete system.

Evidence for general improvements in action understanding is mixed. Several gains in Table 7 are small, three benchmarks regress, and VideoMME action recognition and action reasoning both decline. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates establish the reliability of small gains. Attention comparisons change multiple components simultaneously and therefore do not isolate the action token’s causal effect.

Important reproducibility details remain unclear, including task-mixture and replay proportions, auxiliary-loss weights, and the full multilabel candidate-generation and decoding protocol for Animal Kingdom. Overall, the substantial empirical gains make this a credible borderline submission, but unresolved evaluation issues and limited isolation of the novel components leave it below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful weakness in video MLLMs: distinguishing fine-grained actions among plausible alternatives. Specialist-generated distractors offer a practical benchmark construction strategy, and GPT-4o’s drop from 87.6% with random choices to 52.2% with TIM distractors demonstrates the importance of candidate difficulty.

The training approach produces substantial gains beyond simply adding in-domain data. Table 3 shows 64.4% accuracy with adversarial distractors versus 55.0% with random distractors, while the full model reaches 73.4%. Both additive and leave-one-out ablations are provided.

Evaluation is unusually broad, covering multiple model backbones, four action recognition datasets, and 13 general video benchmarks. Animal Kingdom results, including comparisons against random-choice finetuning on two backbones, provide useful evidence that the approach extends beyond kitchen videos.

The label-only EPIC-KITCHENS result improves on TIM from 56.4% to 58.3%, and the appendix compares the proposed structured prediction pipeline with both an unadapted MLLM reranker and exhaustive candidate scoring.
weaknesses: The strongest EPIC-KITCHENS recognition result has a potentially serious information-access confound. Section 4.3 states that the 63.2% narration setting uses the narration of the corresponding video clip. If the correct candidate receives its test clip’s human annotation while distractors receive narrations from other clips, this supplies privileged instance-specific information unavailable in conventional recognition. Appendix F.1 does not resolve how candidates are constructed without this asymmetry. The 58.3% label-only result is the cleaner comparison.

Benchmark validity needs stronger auditing. Different action classes do not guarantee mutually exclusive descriptions, particularly when narrations mention multiple objects or overlapping actions, as Figure 5 illustrates. There is no systematic human assessment of answer uniqueness, ambiguity rates, or human accuracy, nor a text-only baseline to test candidate-construction shortcuts.

Architectural novelty is modest: the action token combines familiar token aggregation and auxiliary classification, while structured prediction is specialist-guided reranking. Its incremental contribution is also uncertain: removing the action token from the full model reduces accuracy by only 0.5 points in Table 11, without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Comparisons with auxiliary supervision on pooled visual features and direct use of the trained classification heads would better establish its value.

Generalization claims require qualification. Switching from AVION to TIM changes the distractor distribution but retains the same dataset and label space. EPFL’s zero-shot result applies only to the second-stage model because candidates come from a target-dataset specialist. Appendix D also changes both training and testing candidate counts, so declining accuracy cannot isolate overfitting from increased test difficulty.

General video improvements are mostly small and lack uncertainty estimates. Three benchmarks regress, and VideoMME action recognition and action reasoning both decline. These results support largely preserving general capabilities more strongly than broadly improving action understanding.

Important reproducibility details remain underspecified, including task and replay mixture proportions, auxiliary-loss weights, narration sampling and split restrictions, and the adaptation of candidate selection and supervision to Animal Kingdom’s multilabel setting. Overall, the empirical promise is substantial, but the evaluation ambiguities and limited isolation of the novel components leave the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold.
